2015.tone: Heath describes a full Dogon-type tonal system (Sec. 2.1, 3.7): syllable tones H, L, <HL>, <LH>, bell-shaped <LHL> (no <HLH> syllable); lexical stem melodies /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/, /HLH/; verbs lexically /H/ or /LH/; every stem has at least one H-tone; stem-wide tone overlays ({L}, {HL}) imposed by tonosyntactic controllers (adjectives, demonstratives, possessors, relative heads, negative suffixes). A full-text search of the 408-page grammar: 'stress' occurs only twice, both about English ('unstressed clause-final now / mind you'); 'accent' and 'prominen-' never for Ben Tey. Stress/accent is therefore neither asserted nor explicitly denied; the grammar's only prominence talk is metrical (Sec. 3.2.2): initial syllable 'arguably' strong, weak positions show raising/reduction/apocope of short high vowels, and 'metrical structure plays a relatively small role'. Phrase-final intonation (prolongation, dying-quail fall) is treated separately in Sec. 3.8.

tn.quote: Berta is a tone language with two tones, high tone (H) and low tone (L). In a few instances there is a falling tone, and even less often, a rising one. These contours can be explained as a combination of high and low tone together on one tone bearing unit (TBU). While high tone and low tone can appear in any environment, the falling tone is restricted to the last syllable, and appears most often in Arabic loan words. The tone differentiates lexical as well as grammatical meaning.
tn.cite: Neudorf, Susanne. 2016. Phonology of Berta. SIL Language and Culture Archives. Dallas: SIL International. 47 pp.
tn.note: Two tones, high and low, with lexical and grammatical (case, tense, valence) function; rare falling/rising contours are H+L on one syllable, falling mostly final in Arabic loans; stress not by pitch.

2023.dq: Marind roots, as opposed to compounds and inflected forms, invariably take final stress (Drabbe 1955: 16.)
2023.dloc: Usher n.d. 'Marind', raw DokuWiki export saved 2026-09-17, section 'Historical phonology' (syncope preamble)
2023.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the ROOT (realised as a pitch rise, per Drabbe 1955:16 as relayed by Usher); compounds and inflected forms are exempt, so the position is not computable from the syllable count of the word. Drabbe-1954 Mbian citation forms relayed by Usher carry the mark on the last syllable (mi'laf, ma'ndow, ke'maɣ, iz'mi, af'si, wah'ni, hi'kam...). Geurtjens 1933:385 (first-hand): a paragogic e/a added after a closed final syllable is unstressed (abligĕ, afsarĕ), i.e. stress stays on the root-final syllable.
2023.srule: Usher (family-level, diachronic): trisyllabic roots receive secondary stress on the initial syllable beside root-final primary stress; in Mbian the destressed medial vowel was lost, so such roots surface as final-stressed disyllables (*awasi > af'si, *uahani > wah'ni, *ij[e]mi > iz'mi). No placement of secondary or rhythmic stress in synchronic Mbian words is given, and the relayed Drabbe-1954 Mbian forms carry one stress mark each.
2023.quote: Stress falls on the final syllable of the root, as it does in the distantly-related Lowland Ok family to the northeast; Drabbe (1955: 16) characterizes this as a rise in pitch or tone. Trisyllablic roots receive secondary stress on the initial syllable, leading to syncope and the formation of medial consonant clusters in Mbian and Kumb. ... Stress, while not consistently indicated, is shown here because it is sometimes contrastive due to inflection and compounding (Drabbe 1955: 16.) ... Marind roots, as opposed to compounds and inflected forms, invariably take final stress (Drabbe 1955: 16.) …

2027.heavy: Vowel length explicitly denied as a conditioner: 'auch nicht aus Länge oder Kürze der Vokale'.
2027.prule: Main (dynamic) stress falls on one of the last three syllables of the word, but no rule determines which one (vowel quantity explicitly ruled out as a conditioner); stress is marked lexically with accents throughout the texts and vocabulary (vocabulary preamble: where accent marks are missing, stress was not securely determined). Rhythmic constraints: words of 3+ syllables carry at least two stresses, and never more than two syllables in a row stay unstressed ('trochaic-anapaestic' rhythm). A demoted main stress survives as secondary stress under reduplication or when a suffix attracts the main stress.
2027.srule: When the stem is reduplicated or an ending attracts the main stress, the stem's original main stress remains as a secondary stress (Nebenton), so such words of three or more syllables carry at least two stresses (mṓli 'thread' > mṑlimṓli 'string figure'; ibál 'he falls' > ibàlbèhé 'he will not fall'); never more than two consecutive syllables are unstressed ('trochaic-anapaestic' rhythm, scansions p. 235); the 'independent' body-part forms carry a Nebenton on the final syllable (§21). No further placement rule is given.

2030.dq: Although a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables this word within an utterance might change the stress to a different syllable or even lose it in favor of a semantically more important word in the context. Within an utterance it is rather a phrase (whether noun or verb phrase) carrying a stress than single words.
2030.prule: Stress, which always co-occurs with high pitch, is phonemic and lexically contrastive: its position is not predictable from syllable count or weight and distinguishes minimal pairs by position alone (initial vs final 'kókmen vs kok'mén, 'síNam vs si'Nám, 'bókolif vs boko'líf; initial vs medial 'áluue vs a'lúue). No default or positional rule is stated anywhere in the paper; the transcribed word list (sec. 3.3) marks stress on initial, medial or final syllables item by item.

2031.dq: Fifth, stress varies directly as order of occurrence in an utterance. Thus, in a word like ágágá, "many chairs", where other relevant conditions (i.e., level, pitch, length, and sonority) are equal, the first a gets the most stress, the intermediate a intermediate stress, and the last a least stress.
2031.prule: No phonemic stress. Bini is a terrace-tone language with up to six distinctive tones (top, high, mid, low, flat, bottom; most speakers have four or five). Perceived loudness ('phonetic stress') is a gradient by-product ranked 1-6 and correlating, in order of importance, with tone-glide, tone-height, vowel length, vowel sonority and order of occurrence in the utterance (earlier vowel louder when all else is equal). No rule fixes a stress position in the word.
2031.srule: Not mentioned in Wescott 1962, Ch. 2 sec. 3 'Stress' pp. 30-33, sec. 4 p. 36, sec. 7 'Prosodic Phonemes' pp. 51-57: the source denies phonemic stress altogether ('Although it has no phonemic stress, Bini... does have phonetic stress', p. 30) and grades loudness on a 1-6 phonetic scale by tone-glide, tone-height, length and sonority, so no primary/secondary word stress is posited.

2031.tone: Wescott 1962 p. 56: 'Bini, like Ibo (but unlike Yoruba), is what Welmers calls a terrace-tone language'; p. 57: 'only about one out of ten Bini really have six distinctive tones. About three out of ten, in fact, have only four distinctive tones (top, high, low, and flat; mid having merged with high and bottom with flat). The remaining six out of ten have five distinctive tones'. On stress (p. 30): 'Although it has no phonemic stress, Bini, like all other known languages, does have phonetic stress', a loudness scale driven first by tone-glide and tone-height; p. 57 mentions stress only as co-varying with pitch ('the syllable -ghe is minimal in both pitch and stress, while -gie has audibly higher pitch and stronger stress'). Later descriptions held (Emovon 1979, Omozuwa 1989, 1991, Adeniyi 2007, Ogie 2009, Agheyisi 1986) treat Edo as a two-tone (H, L) language with downstep and say nothing about word stress; Manfredi 2003 is a theoretical accentual (trochaic-foot) reanalysis of the tone, not a descriptive stress statement.

2032.prule: Tone language: five 'well-distinguished' pitch levels (overhoog, hoog, middelhoog, laag, overlaag, compared to harmonium notes mi, re, do#, do, si) plus rising and falling contours, with lexical ('semantische') and grammatical tone rules for nouns (pp. 262-268) and verbs (1949: 172-194). Stress ('intensiteitsaccent') is a secondary, unwritten, tone-derived prominence stated for nouns only: it falls on the first stem vowel ('eerste kernklinker') if that vowel is high-toned; if it is low-toned, the (syllabic CV) class prefix is stressed if there is one; nouns with the nasal (n-) prefix stress the first stem vowel. Examples as printed: d'ikama 'foot', g'ulandúlá 'to follow', k'u'tú [scan-garbled; kutú on p. 267] 'scorpion', ŋg'undú 'brook-garden', pl. m'angundu. No positional stress rule computable from syllable count or weight; no stress statement for verbs.

2034.tone: Privative word-tone system: /H/ vs toneless (realised L); mora is the TBU (short V = 1 mora, long V/diphthong = 2; consonants non-moraic). Each word has exactly one of four melodies H, LH, HL, LHL, so H is obligatory and culminative per word; the point where the melody switches level (the 'diacritic accent' in Hyman's/Donohue's sense) is lexical and unpredictable (eeqa 'banana' vs eeqa 'I myself', p.18; minimal pairs aku/aku, muri/muri, nari/nari p.18). The author explicitly says the diacritic accent 'does not mark prominence of a mora or syllable, as stress-accent does', that 'Binumarien moras do not have a hierarchy of prominence' (p.19), and that the system 'lacks metricality: to my knowledge, there is no hierarchy of strong and weak syllables' (p.17), repeated as 'does not feature metricality' (p.25) and 'does not exhibit metricality' (p.58). Utterance level: at least one H per utterance (default H on the utterance-final mora when no lexical H is realised) and downstep (sec. 3.4). Verbs not analysed for tone. Oatridge & Oatridge 1966 sec. 2.2: 'Binumarien has a system of register tones which show only two significant levels... Each vowel is of one mora of length and carries its own register tone'; the word 'stress' never occurs in that paper. No stress of any degree is posited by any held source.
